titulo.texto: Traditional Totonac Men’s Clothing from Papantla

frase_gancho.texto: All-white clothing, with a red kerchief, from the land of vanilla.

puente_narrativo.texto: From clothing, we move on to the festival with a mask. Look for a black wooden mask, smiling, with a mustache, and a straw hat covered in colorful ribbons.

guion_corto.texto: This is the traditional dress of Totonac men from Papantla, in northern Veracruz. It is made of white cotton muslin: loose trousers, tied at the waist and at the ankles, and a long shirt. The only thing that breaks the white is a bright red kerchief tied at the neck, and sometimes a palm hat and leather huaraches. It is clothing made for the heat and humidity of the Gulf, and it is worn at festivals and ceremonies. Totonac women, for their part, wear white skirts and a light, embroidered quechquémitl. In a region of jungle, sea and rivers, the color white is cool, clean and elegant.

guion_largo.texto:
A man in white, with a red kerchief at his neck. This is how you recognize a Totonac from Papantla, in a plaza or on a road. The outfit is simple, but it has a particular elegance, made of whiteness and contrast. And it is an invitation to talk about a fascinating region, the land of vanilla.

Papantla is in northern Veracruz, in a region of heat and humidity where white has a practical purpose: it reflects the sun and keeps you cool. The outfit is made of cotton muslin, with loose trousers that are tied at the waist and ankles, and a long-sleeved shirt. The red kerchief, a touch of bright color, is knotted at the neck or crossed over the chest. Sometimes it is completed with a hand-woven palm hat and with huaraches.

Totonac women dress in white as well: a wrapped skirt and a quechquémitl of very light fabric, embroidered with flowers. So when a Totonac family gathers for a festival, it looks as if a white cloud had come down to the plaza. And it is in that plaza where you have so often seen what you saw in the Puebla Highlands hall: the Voladores (Flyers), in their red and colorful costumes, spinning from the top of a pole.

Papantla is also the world capital of vanilla. This plant, an orchid, is native to this region, and the Totonacs were among the first to cultivate and use it. The Mexica received it as tribute to flavor cacao. Imagine the chocolate of kings with vanilla: two products of Mexico that today travel all over the world.

There is an astonishing story. For centuries, only in Mexico could vanilla be made to bear fruit, because here it is pollinated by some very particular bees. When the plant was taken to other places, it did not produce pods. Until, in the year one thousand eight hundred forty-one, a young enslaved man from the island of Réunion, named Edmond Albius, discovered how to pollinate it by hand, and that technique is still used today all over the world. In this way Mexico lost the monopoly of a product that had been its own for centuries.

Near Papantla is El Tajín, one of the most impressive cities of antiquity on the Gulf, where the yokes and the palmate stones you saw in the Gulf Coast Hall come from. Its Pyramid of the Niches has hundreds of recesses, and it has been compared to a calendar in stone. Today's Totonacs feel that city as part of their history, and its name, Tajín, is usually translated as “thunder” or “lightning.”

Imagine the outfit in motion. When the son plays and the dancers stamp their feet, the trousers sway, the red kerchief flies and all the white clothing seems to float. In Papantla, the great festival of Corpus Christi, around the month of June, fills the streets with people dressed this way.

The white outfit is, then, one piece of a complete landscape: the heat, the vanilla, the voladores, the city of stone. Behind its simplicity lies a way of living in which elegance is also cleanliness, freshness and respect.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Vanilla is a European invention.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is an orchid native to Mexico, and the Totonacs were among the first to cultivate and use it.
